lesson.text: Quick memory: what should a fair judge do before deciding? (Listen to both sides.) Reading the news needs the same skill. Today: how to tell a fact from an opinion, and why one story can have different sides.

A fact can be checked and shown to be true: 'The bridge opened on Monday.' An opinion is what someone thinks or feels: 'The bridge is ugly.' Opinions can be sensible, but they cannot be proved true or false.

Clue words help: 'I think', 'I believe', 'best', 'worst', 'should' and 'beautiful' often show an opinion. Numbers, dates and things that happened can usually be checked, but even a fact can be wrong, so check it.

News reports tell what happened: who, what, where, when, why and how. Good reporters check facts with more than one source and keep their own opinion out. Opinion pieces and reviews share a writer's view, and should say so.
One event can have different sides. A new road may help drivers get to work faster, but upset people who lose a park. Both views can be honest. A fair report gives both sides and lets you decide.
Before you believe or share a story, ask: who wrote it, and why? Is it news, an opinion or an advert? What do other sources say? Does the headline match the story? Online, anyone can post anything.
Sort sentences by asking: could I check it? 'The park opened in 2019' can be checked, so it is a fact (true or not). 'It is the best park' is a judgement, so it is an opinion.
Try it in the world: write a short news sign about something that happened in your world: who, what, where and when. Put your opinion of it on a separate sign. Next: many cultures, one community.

choices: The river is the prettiest place.
exercises.explain: 'The river is 12 km long' can be checked by measuring; the others are opinions.

exercises.hint: Look for a clue word like 'best'.
choices: There are 7 days in a week.
exercises.explain: 'Summer is the best season' is what someone feels; the others can be checked.

exercises.prompt: An opinion can be proved true or false.
exercises.hint: Can you prove that a song is the best?
exercises.explain: False: opinions are what people think or feel; they cannot be proved.

exercises.prompt: Which word often shows an opinion?
exercises.explain: 'Best' is a judgement, so it often shows an opinion.

exercises.prompt: Good reporters check their facts with more than one source.
exercises.hint: Why would one source not be enough?
exercises.explain: True: checking more than one source catches mistakes.

items: Chess is more fun than football.
exercises.hint: Could you check it? Look for judging words like 'beautifully' and 'should'.
exercises.explain: Facts: the score, the castle's date, 28 pupils. Opinions: played beautifully, more fun, should be banned.

exercises.prompt: What does a news report tell you?
choices: who, what, where, when, why and how
exercises.explain: Who, what, where, when, why and how: what happened.

exercises.prompt: A new road will be built through a park. Which is the fairest report?
exercises.hint: Who is affected by the road?
choices: it gives the views of drivers and park users
it says the road is terrible
exercises.explain: A fair report gives both sides: the drivers who gain and the people who lose the park.

exercises.prompt: Why might a headline be misleading?
exercises.hint: Headlines want you to read on.
choices: it may grab attention more than tell the truth
it is too short to read
exercises.explain: Headlines are written to grab attention, so read the whole story before you believe it.

exercises.prompt: Two people can see the same event and honestly give different views.
exercises.hint: Think of the road and the park.
exercises.explain: True: people who are affected in different ways can honestly see it differently.

exercises.prompt: 'Scientists found 4 new kinds of frog, and they are the cutest ever.' Which part is an opinion?
exercises.hint: Which part could not be checked?
exercises.explain: 'The cutest ever' is a judgement; the rest can be checked.

exercises.prompt: You see a shocking story online. What should you do first?
choices: check who wrote it and what others say
believe it because it is online
exercises.explain: Check who wrote it and why, and compare with other sources, before believing or sharing it.

exercises.prompt: Put these checks in a sensible order before sharing a story.
exercises.hint: Decide last, after you have checked.
items: check who wrote it and why
read the whole story, not just the headline
exercises.explain: Read it all, check the writer, compare sources, then decide.

choices: a writer's opinion of a book or film
exercises.explain: A review shares a writer's opinion of a book, a film, a show or a game.

exercises.prompt: If a story has numbers in it, it must be true.
exercises.hint: Can numbers be made up or wrong?
exercises.explain: False: numbers can be wrong or made up. 'Our town has 2 million dragons' has a number, but it is not true. Check numbers with another source, as with any fact.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of text to what it does.
exercises.explain: A news report tells what happened, an opinion piece shares a view, and an advert wants you to buy.

exercises.prompt: Which often show an opinion, and which can be checked?
exercises.hint: Could you look it up or measure it?
exercises.explain: 'I think' and 'the best' show opinions; a date and a length can be checked.

exercises.prompt: A news report: the mayor opened a playground beside the river on Monday. Match each question to its answer.
matches: to give children a place to play
exercises.hint: A news report answers who, what, where, when, why and how.
exercises.explain: Who: the town's mayor. Where: beside the river. When: on Monday. Why: to give children a place to play.

exercises.prompt: A report on the new park. Sort the sentences: a fact that can be checked, or an opinion?
items: It is the loveliest park in town.
The slide is far too small.
The mayor cut a ribbon at 10:00.
exercises.hint: Ask: could I check it? A wrong fact is still a fact claim, not an opinion.
exercises.explain: Checked: the date, the ribbon at 10:00, and 4,000 swings (easy to check, and probably wrong!). Opinions: loveliest, should visit, and far too small are judgements.
